q: Frozen fruit is picked before dawn on a January morning and pressed while still solid. What is being separated from what?
opts: Yeast from the must, which the cold kills off
Skins from pulp, which the cold makes easier to part
Sugar from acid, with the acid left behind in the ice
Water held as ice crystals, from concentrated sugary juice
exp: The ice stays behind in the press and only the concentrated liquid runs out. German rules set a minimum of minus seven degrees Celsius at picking, and the wine keeps ferocious acidity alongside its sugar.

q: Eiswein and Beerenauslese reach comparable must weights, yet one condition sets Eiswein apart. Which?
opts: Its grapes must be picked before the general harvest starts
It must be fermented out to complete dryness
Its grapes must be healthy and free of noble rot, and frozen on the vine
It must spend three years in cask before release
exp: Botrytis is what concentrates a Beerenauslese; freezing is what concentrates an Eiswein, and rot would muddy the clean piercing fruit that is the whole appeal of the style. The gamble is that a hard enough frost may never arrive.

q: Pickers go through the vineyard taking only the ripest bunches, some of them touched by noble rot. Which Pradikat does that describe?
opts: Kabinett
Spatlese
Auslese
Trockenbeerenauslese
exp: Auslese means selected, and at this rung the selection is made bunch by bunch. Beerenauslese goes further and picks individual berries, and Trockenbeerenauslese takes only the shrivelled ones.

q: German wine law stacks four broad quality tiers. Which sequence runs from the bottom upward?
opts: Deutscher Wein, Qualitatswein, Landwein, Pradikatswein
Deutscher Wein, Landwein, Qualitatswein, Pradikatswein
Landwein, Deutscher Wein, Pradikatswein, Qualitatswein
Qualitatswein, Landwein, Pradikatswein, Deutscher Wein
exp: The two lower tiers are table and country wine. The two upper ones must name an Anbaugebiet and pass an official tasting and analysis, and Pradikatswein is then split by must weight into the six familiar rungs.

q: A German Riesling labelled trocken may legally carry up to nine grams of residual sugar rather than the usual four. What has to be true for that to be allowed?
opts: The alcohol must exceed thirteen percent
The wine must be at least three years old
The wine must come from a classified single vineyard
The total acidity must be no more than two grams below the residual sugar
exp: The allowance exists because acidity masks sugar on the palate. Nine grams in a taut, high-acid Riesling still tastes dry, where the same sugar in a soft low-acid wine would not.

q: Many German estates now put a word on their off-dry bottles that carries no legal meaning whatever, in preference to halbtrocken. Which word?
opts: Suss
Feinherb
Edelsuss
Lieblich
exp: Halbtrocken is capped at twelve grams of residual sugar, or eighteen where the sugar sits no more than ten grams above the total acidity, and it sounds like a compromise, so growers reached for something warmer. Feinherb is undefined and therefore covers a wider range, while lieblich and suss are the legal terms for genuinely sweet wine.

q: Two Mosel labels read Piesporter Goldtropfchen and Piesporter Michelsberg, and the two look identical in form. What separates them?
opts: One denotes a dry wine and the other a sweet one
One names a village and the other names a district
Goldtropfchen is a collective name and Michelsberg a single vineyard
Goldtropfchen is one vineyard, Michelsberg many
exp: An Einzellage is one delimited site; a Grosslage can spread across thousands of hectares and many villages, and nothing in the pre-reform wording tells them apart. The 2021 law now requires a Grosslage name to be prefixed Region, phased in toward the 2026 vintage, but older bottles on shelves and lists still carry the ambiguous form.

q: Thousands of small German vineyard names were abolished and merged by one piece of legislation, which also invented the collective site. Which law?
opts: The German Wine Law of 1971
The German Wine Law of 1930
The EU wine market reform of 2008
The VDP statutes of 1910
exp: The 1971 law cut some thirty thousand site names down to around two and a half thousand Einzellagen and imposed a minimum size on them. It also created the Grosslage, which let a bulk blend borrow a famous village's name.

q: A semi-sweet German white sold under brand names for a generation takes its name from a church in Worms. Which wine?
opts: Piesporter Michelsberg
Kroever Nacktarsch
Liebfraumilch
Zeller Schwarze Katz
exp: The Liebfrauenkirche gave its name to a Qualitatswein blend carrying at least eighteen grams of residual sugar and drawn from Rheinhessen, the Pfalz, the Nahe or the Rheingau. Its collapse in reputation dragged German wine down with it for thirty years.

q: A dry wine from a member estate's top classified site carries the letters GG embossed in the glass, and an eagle bearing a grape cluster on the capsule. What is that marking?
opts: A legal German quality tier ranking above Pradikatswein
A promise of at least ten years of bottle age before release
A guarantee that the fruit was affected by noble rot
Grosses Gewachs, the mark of a growers' association
exp: The VDP is an association of growers and its rulebook is stricter than the law, capping yields, requiring hand harvest and holding the wine back for a later release. The 2021 wine law has since written Grosses Gewachs into German law as well, with the qualifying rules set region by region, but the embossed bottle and the eagle capsule remain the VDP's own. Grosses Gewachs is always dry; a sweet wine off the same site is labelled with its Pradikat instead.

q: The VDP grades its members' wines on a four-step pyramid modelled on Burgundy. What sits at the top of it?
opts: VDP.Erste Lage
VDP.Grosse Lage
VDP.Ortswein
VDP.Gutswein
exp: Gutswein is the estate wine and Ortswein the village wine, with the two site tiers above them. Grosse Lage answers to a Grand Cru, and it is where Grosses Gewachs comes from.

q: Reference books on vine varieties give a single plant one main entry and then list a dozen further names beneath it, every one of them in daily use somewhere. What is each of those further names called?
opts: A synonym
A crossing
A rootstock
A clone
exp: A synonym is the identical plant under another name, so two wines can share a vine and share nothing else whatever. A clone is a selection made within one variety and a crossing is a new variety bred from two parents, so neither word will do instead. The most travelled vines have collected names by the dozen, and the registers that hold them run to hundreds of pages.

q: Cuttings travelled with growers, soldiers and monks for centuries before anybody kept a register of what was planted where. What is the lasting consequence for today's labels?
opts: Each district ended up with a genuinely different variety of its own
Most European varieties died out and a handful of survivors replaced them
One variety turns up under a different name in nearly every country that took it up
Grape names were standardised early, because the export trade insisted on it
exp: A vine arriving somewhere new was named in the local language, or after the place it had come from, or after whoever carried the cuttings, and nothing obliged anyone to ask what it had been called before. Naming was local and the plant was not, which is the entire reason synonym lists exist. It also means the number of distinct varieties in the world is far smaller than the number of names for them.

q: Two districts a thousand miles apart argue over whether their grape is one variety or two, and the wines taste nothing alike. What settles it?
opts: Tasting the two wines side by side
Comparing the colour of the berries at harvest
Comparing the DNA profiles of the two plants
Taking whichever of the two names was recorded first
exp: A profile is read from the vine rather than from the wine, so climate, yield and cellar work cannot disturb it. That matters because those three move flavour far more than identity does, and no argument of this kind has ever been settled by tasting. The older evidence was the shape of the leaves and the growing tips, skilled work that was frequently wrong.

q: A grower knows his vine by three names and may print only one of them on the bottles he is sending abroad. What decides which?
opts: The importer chooses whichever of the names sells best in that market
The name used in the variety's country of origin always takes precedence
The oldest recorded name has to be used wherever the wine is sold
Each country publishes the variety names its own labels are allowed to carry
exp: Each country keeps its own list of the variety names its labels may carry, and a name missing from that list cannot go on a bottle sold there. The same wine can therefore be sold under one name at home and a different one across a border. A producer who exports widely reprints labels market by market for exactly this reason.

q: A variety name printed for generations was struck off the permitted list because it repeated the name of a protected wine region elsewhere. Which principle forced the change?
opts: A variety name has to be in the language of the country that grows it
A variety name has to match the one used where the variety originated
A variety name may not run to more than a single word
A variety name may not trade on somebody else's protected place name
exp: Protection of a place name reaches evocation as well as outright use, so a variety name that reads like a region can be withdrawn even where nobody was deceived. Growers are normally given a transition period to sell through old labels, which leaves cellars holding bottles under a name the shelf no longer shows. Changes of this kind have gone through more than once in the last twenty-five years.
